blocks.text: A tanker driver in Lagos says he delivered "30,000 litres". A physicist writing the same figure in SI units would write $30\,\text{m}^3$. Both describe the same fuel, but only one of them can be dropped straight into an equation. Physics needs one agreed system of units, and the whole system is built from just seven quantities.

blocks.markdown:
A **physical quantity** is anything you can measure. Every measurement has two parts: a **number** and a **unit**. Writing 5 for a length is meaningless — 5 metres, 5 centimetres and 5 kilometres are wildly different.

The international agreement we use is the **SI system** (Système International d'Unités). Its cleverness is that it starts with only seven **fundamental** (base) quantities. Everything else is **derived** from them by multiplying and dividing.

blocks.title: Fundamental and derived quantities
blocks.text: A fundamental quantity cannot be expressed in terms of any other physical quantity — it is defined independently. A derived quantity is obtained by combining two or more fundamental quantities, so its unit is a combination of base units.

blocks.caption: The seven fundamental SI quantities. Learn all seven — they are asked directly in WAEC and NECO.

blocks.markdown:
### Building derived units

To find a derived unit, write the defining equation and substitute base units.

Speed is $\text{distance} \div \text{time}$, so its unit is $\text{m}/\text{s} = \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Acceleration is $\text{velocity} \div \text{time}$, giving $\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}$. Force is $\text{mass} \times \text{acceleration}$, so the newton is really $\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}$.

blocks.markdown:
### SI prefixes

Prefixes let you avoid long strings of zeros. $0.000\,45\ \text{m}$ becomes $0.45\ \text{mm}$; $3\,000\,000\ \text{W}$ becomes $3\ \text{MW}$.

When you substitute into a formula, **always convert back to base units first**. A resistance in $\text{k}\Omega$ and a current in $\text{mA}$ will give the wrong answer unless both are converted.

blocks.caption: SI prefixes that appear most often in secondary physics

blocks.title: Squared and cubed prefixes
blocks.text: 1 cm is 10⁻² m, but 1 cm³ is (10⁻²)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, not 10⁻² m³. Cube or square the whole conversion factor, not just the number. Forgetting this is the single most common unit-conversion error in density questions.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: "Which of the following is not a fundamental quantity?" is almost guaranteed. Weight, force, density, pressure, energy, area and volume are all derived. Only length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity are fundamental.

points: Every measurement is a number together with a unit — never quote one without the other.
There are seven fundamental SI quantities: length, mass, time, current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.
A derived quantity is built from fundamental ones; find its unit by substituting base units into its defining equation.
1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻², 1 W = 1 kg m² s⁻³ and 1 Pa = 1 kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
Convert every value to base SI units before substituting into a formula, and remember to cube or square prefixes for volumes and areas.
